items.topic: Position limits as a hedge against model risk
items.definition: A position limit is a cap on how much exposure a trading desk can build up in a given type of trading, used to bound the damage any single flawed model can cause.
items.core_idea: Since no valuation model can be fully trusted, firms cap the amount of risk any one trading strategy or desk can carry, so that if that model turns out to be wrong, the resulting loss is contained rather than catastrophic.
key_points: No model can be completely trusted, so risk controls should assume any given model could eventually be shown to be wrong.
Position limits enforce diversification across trading types rather than concentrating risk based on one model's output.
The goal is bounding worst-case loss from a single point of model failure, not improving the model's accuracy.
relationships: Complements modeling reserves as a second, independent layer of model-risk control.
trading_implications: A desk should not size positions purely off one model's confidence, since the limit exists precisely because that confidence could be misplaced.

source.section_hint: 6.4 Model Risk - Model Overlays and Reserves

items.definition: A modeling reserve is a portion of a model's reported profit that is deliberately withheld from recognized earnings for some period, to absorb losses if the model later proves flawed.
items.core_idea: A model that shows a steady stream of profits attracts less scrutiny than one losing money, so it is more likely to have an undiscovered flaw; setting aside part of its profits as a reserve protects against that hidden risk before it is caught.
key_points: Models that are hemorrhaging money draw attention and get their problems found quickly.
A steadily profitable model is more dangerous precisely because it is more likely to be left unexamined.
The reserve is not recognized as earnings until the model has proven itself over some operating period.
This is described as a second way (alongside position limits) of limiting model risk.
relationships: A response to the same underlying model risk that position limits address, but targets underscrutinized profitable models rather than exposure size.
trading_implications: Consistently profitable models should not be assumed safe just because they aren't losing money; reserving part of their P&L is a deliberate hedge against undetected model error.
common_misunderstandings: It would be a mistake to assume a model showing steady profits is lower risk than one showing losses — the source frames it as the more dangerous case because it is less likely to be scrutinized.

source.section_hint: 6.4 Model Risk - Model Overlays and Reserves / Common Terms

items.definition: A model overlay is a manual adjustment applied to a model's output by someone outside the model itself, used to impose a firm's own judgment on top of the model's calculation.
items.core_idea: Firm management can override or scale a model's output from the outside — for example, deliberately doubling a worst-case loss estimate to be more conservative — without changing the model's internal logic.
key_points: The overlay comes from an external source (e.g., firm management), not from the model's own calculation.
The example given is management doubling the risk team's worst-case loss estimate to get a more conservative figure.
It is presented as a discrete tool distinct from both position limits and modeling reserves.
relationships: One of the named tools/terms under model risk controls, alongside modeling reserve.
trading_implications: Risk figures reported to a firm's leadership may already reflect a deliberate conservative adjustment layered on top of the raw model output, not the model's unadjusted number.
